answer: The JSON provider in src/flask/json/provider.py exposes an ensure_ascii attribute on DefaultJSONProvider, which defaults to True. The provider passes it through to json.dumps, so when it is True every non-ASCII character in the serialized output is escaped as a \uXXXX sequence and the output is pure ASCII. Setting app.json.ensure_ascii to False makes the serializer emit the raw Unicode characters instead. The value only changes the textual form of the output; the decoded data is identical either way, so round-tripping through json.loads gives the same Python objects. The flask.json.dumps helper and jsonify both route through the provider's dumps method, so the setting applies to every JSON response produced by the app.

Blueprint in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py keeps a private boolean named _got_registered_once. It starts as False and is set to True the first time the blueprint is passed to Flask.register_blueprint for any app. Setup methods such as add_url_rule, before_request, errorhandler and record call a guard (_check_setup_finished) that checks this flag and raises an AssertionError when it is set. The guard exists because the deferred functions stored by those methods are replayed only at registration time, so a route added after registration would silently never be installed on the app. Raising early turns that silent failure into a visible error that tells the developer to move the code before register_blueprint.

Static file serving is split out of the core app by the Blueprint and the scaffold layer. A Blueprint or Flask application created with a static_folder argument calls add_url_rule for a catch-all route built from static_url_path and the endpoint name static, and the view delegates to send_from_directory in src/flask/helpers.py. Because the static route is registered through the same add_url_rule and deferred-setup machinery as any other route, it behaves like ordinary routing. Caching is kept consistent by reading the max age through get_send_file_max_age, which checks SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT on the current app. Both the application and each blueprint call that same method, so their static responses share one cache policy controlled by config.

UnexpectedUnicodeError in src/flask/debughelpers.py is declared as a subclass of both AssertionError and UnicodeError. It is raised only in debug mode, in place of the plain UnicodeError that Werkzeug would otherwise produce, when request form data or uploaded content is decoded with the wrong encoding. The UnicodeError base keeps it compatible with code that catches encoding problems, so existing handlers still behave as expected. The AssertionError base marks it as a developer-facing diagnostic: it signals that the application has a programming mistake, such as reading a body as text when it is binary, rather than bad client input. This separates development-time validation failures from ordinary encoding failures inside Flask's layered design.

The subdomain test in tests/test_basic.py (test_subdomain_matching) forms a chain of four steps. First, the test sets the SERVER_NAME config value, which Flask uses as the base domain when binding the URL map. Second, a route is registered with a subdomain argument, which Werkzeug stores on the Rule object in the url_map. Third, a request is built with a base_url or host that includes the subdomain, such as kb.localhost, through app.test_client or app.test_request_context. Fourth, that request context calls create_url_adapter in src/flask/app.py, which binds the URL map to the request's server name and subdomain so Werkzeug can match the rule. Only if all four links agree does the view resolve.

Template helpers registered on a blueprint, such as template_filter, template_global and template_test, are stored as deferred functions through Blueprint.record_once. When the blueprint is registered with an app, each deferred function runs with a BlueprintSetupState, and the callback writes into app.jinja_env, the shared Jinja2 Environment that the app creates in create_jinja_environment in src/flask/app.py. Because the write happens on that single environment object, every template rendered by the app sees the helper, regardless of which blueprint the template came from. The record_once wrapper prevents the same helper from being installed twice if the blueprint is registered repeatedly. Rendering uses the app environment, so the helpers are visible without any per-blueprint environment.

The test helper class in the test suite that stands in for a pathlib.Path implements the __fspath__ dunder method. When the standard library function os.fspath is called on such an object, which open() and other path-accepting functions do internally, Python calls __fspath__, and the helper returns the underlying path as a plain string. That string is the value the standard library then uses. The method is what makes the helper a valid path-like object, so the test can check that Flask accepts any os.PathLike input and converts it to a string before using it. Returning a str is required by the protocol; returning bytes or a non-string would raise a TypeError.

The exception-raising test in tests/test_cli.py is parametrized over pairs of import names and app names, such as a module that does not exist, a module with an import error, or a name that is not an attribute of the module. Each case feeds the pair into the app-locating function in src/flask/cli.py, which is locate_app. That function resolves the import string through prepare_import and import_string, and when the module or attribute is missing it raises NoAppException with a descriptive message. Import failures are wrapped the same way so the CLI reports one consistent error type instead of a raw ImportError. The parametrization checks that every failure path ends in the same exception class, which is what makes the application location function fail predictably for the user.

The test helper FlaskCliRunner is defined in src/flask/testing.py and subclasses click.testing.CliRunner. It is created by Flask.test_cli_runner. Its invoke method wraps the Click call and supplies an obj argument that is a ScriptInfo object whose create_app callable returns the test application. ScriptInfo, defined in src/flask/cli.py, is responsible for loading the app; its load_app method calls the create_app callable first and falls back to importing an app path when no factory is set. Because the runner injects the ScriptInfo through Click's context object, the command runs against the already-built test app without reading FLASK_APP or any environment variable. The result is an isolated command invocation that uses the same app instance as the test.

The tuple tag in src/flask/json/tag.py is a TagTuple whose to_json method returns a list built by calling self.serializer.tag on each item. TaggedJSONSerializer.tag then walks its ordered tag list, calls check on each tag, and for the first match calls that tag's to_json, which can again call serializer.tag on nested items. So a nested tuple causes another round of tagging, and the depth of the recursion equals the depth of the data. The serializer has no visited-set or cycle detection. A tuple cannot refer to itself directly, but a list that contains a tuple which contains the same list can form a cycle, and in that case the recursion never ends and Python raises RecursionError. The risk therefore comes from circular data, not from ordinary nested tuples.

The test class that isolates request context lifecycle from streaming logic is a pytest class in the Flask suite, most likely in tests/test_reqctx.py or tests/test_basic.py, that groups tests around stream_with_context. The pattern is a separation of concerns: one group of tests checks that the request context stays pushed for the whole life of a generator, while the streaming behavior itself is exercised by building a generator and iterating it through the test client. Fixtures create the app and client so each test gets a fresh application. The tests assert that after the response is returned the context is popped and that accessing request inside the generator still works. This keeps lifecycle checks separate from response content checks, so a failure points to the right layer.

The decorator is after_this_request in src/flask/helpers.py. It appends the function to a list named _after_request_functions stored on the active RequestContext, and that list is consumed later in Flask.process_response, which runs during finalize_request. This creates a hidden coupling: the registration depends on a request context being active, so calling it outside a request raises an error, and the callbacks run only if the response pipeline reaches process_response. If the view is nested inside another decorator or registration happens conditionally, the callback order depends on when the code runs, not on where it is written. Functions registered during an error path can also be skipped if handling ends before the normal response stage. The hidden state lives on the context, so the response lifecycle silently owns the decorator's behavior.

The wrapper is _lazy_sha1 in src/flask/sessions.py. It is a small function that takes the data and calls hashlib.sha1 only when it is invoked, rather than referencing hashlib.sha1 at module import. The default digest method for the secure cookie signing serializer is set to this wrapper, not to hashlib.sha1 directly. The reason is that some FIPS-restricted Python builds do not provide SHA-1 at all. Had Flask stored the function object at import, importing flask would fail before the developer could choose a different digest method in configuration. Deferring the lookup means the failure, if any, happens only when a session is actually signed, and an application that sets its own digest method never triggers SHA-1 access.

The decorator is copy_current_request_context in src/flask/ctx.py. It calls the current RequestContext's copy method, which builds a new RequestContext that shares the same request object and the same session mapping reference, so session data reads and writes made in the worker see the original values. The wrapper pushes this copied context inside the worker thread or greenlet and pops it when the wrapped function returns, so request, session and url_adapter work there. Each execution context gets its own context object, so the stack state is isolated per thread. The app context is handled separately by the copy logic, which pushes a context for the same application. The design lets background work use request data safely while keeping the stack of each concurrent execution independent.

The conversion is CertParamType.convert in src/flask/cli.py. It first tries click.Path with exists=True, dir_okay=False and resolve_path=True, so an existing file path is accepted and returned as an absolute path. If that raises BadParameter, the value is lowercased and compared to the string adhoc; when it matches, the method first checks that cryptography is installed and returns the string so Werkzeug can create a self-signed certificate. Otherwise it treats the value as a dotted import path and calls import_string with silent=True. If the imported object is an ssl.SSLContext, that object is returned. Any other result re-raises the original BadParameter, so the option gives a clear error for an unusable value.

Blueprint.add_app_template_filter in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py calls self.record_once with a callback that writes the filter into the app's jinja_env.filters dictionary. The callback is a deferred function, so it is not run when the decorator executes but when the blueprint is registered on the app. Its target is the app-wide environment, not anything tied to the blueprint, so the URL prefix never affects it. The url_prefix passed to register_blueprint is stored on the BlueprintSetupState and used only when building URL rules, so the filter stays visible in every template regardless of the prefix. Because the filter is stored on the shared environment, any template rendered by the app can use it by name, even if the template belongs to a different blueprint.

TagBytes in src/flask/json/tag.py handles bytes by converting them to a JSON-safe string. Its to_json method calls base64.b64encode on the bytes and decodes the result as ASCII, and to_python calls b64decode on the stored string to recover the original bytes. The tag key is a reserved single-key dictionary, so the encoded value is marked as bytes and can be restored when the JSON is parsed. Base64 is a bijective mapping for any byte sequence, so encoding followed by decoding always returns exactly the original bytes, with no loss from padding or encoding choice. Since the tag records the type, the round trip is reversible even though the output is plain text. This is how session values containing binary data survive being stored in a signed cookie.

The method is Flask.handle_exception in src/flask/app.py. It first checks the propagate_exceptions property, which returns the PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS config value when it is set, and otherwise returns True when TESTING or DEBUG is enabled. When propagation is on, the method re-raises the original exception so the test client or debugger can show the traceback. When it is off, the method logs the exception through log_exception, builds an InternalServerError, and passes it to finalize_request with from_error_handler set to True, so the client gets an HTTP 500 response. An application-level error handler for the 500 code is still tried before the default body is produced. The decision therefore depends on configuration state, not on the type of exception.

Blueprint.add_url_rule in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py does not register the rule immediately. It calls self.record with a lambda taking one argument, the setup state s, and that lambda calls s.add_url_rule with the rule, endpoint, view function and options. The record method appends that function to self.deferred_functions. The blueprint has no app yet, and the endpoint must be prefixed with the blueprint name and combined with the url_prefix, which is known only when register_blueprint runs. Deferring the call lets the same blueprint be registered on several apps or with different prefixes, each time replaying the list with fresh state. The lambda captures the arguments, so no work happens until the blueprint is actually attached to an application.

SecureCookieSession in src/flask/sessions.py inherits from werkzeug's CallbackDict, which takes an on_update callback that runs whenever the dictionary is mutated. The session sets this callback to a method that marks the session as modified and accessed. Any write to the session therefore flips the modified flag, which SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session checks at the end of the request to decide whether to send a new Set-Cookie header. The in-memory dictionary is the only copy during the request, and the cookie is written once from it in process_response, so the two cannot drift within one request. Each request gets its own session object loaded from its own cookie, so concurrent requests do not share mutable state; the last response to set the cookie wins for the client.

The namespace is _AppCtxGlobals in src/flask/ctx.py, the object that backs the g proxy. Each AppContext creates one instance in its constructor, and the app context is stored in a ContextVar named _cv_app. Because ContextVar values are copied per thread and per asyncio task, each thread or task sees its own app context and therefore its own g object. The class itself has no lock and no thread-local storage; isolation comes entirely from the contextvars mechanism. Two threads that push separate app contexts for the same application get independent g namespaces, while code within one context shares it. This makes g safe to use without locks across concurrent requests, but data placed on g is not shared between contexts, which is why it is meant for per-request or per-context data.

The _AppCtxGlobals class in src/flask/ctx.py chooses behavior per method. __getattr__ and __delattr__ raise AttributeError when a name is missing, which matches normal Python attribute semantics and makes hasattr and getattr-with-default work as expected. The pop method and the get method take an optional default instead, so a missing key returns that default without an error; pop uses a private sentinel object so that passing None as a real default is still distinct from no default. The __delattr__ implementation deletes from the instance dictionary and converts the KeyError into AttributeError. The design therefore keeps attribute syntax strict while the dictionary-style methods stay lenient, so developers can choose the failure mode at each call site.

The return annotation is built from ResponseReturnValue and related aliases in src/flask/typing.py. The alias unions types such as str, bytes, dict, Response and tuples of a body, a status and headers. A plain dict is accepted because make_response converts it to a JSON response through the app's json provider, so the view returns data and the framework owns serialization. The status code is not part of the dict; it is supplied in a separate tuple element, or via a Response object. This separates the payload type from the HTTP status, so the annotation can describe the body independently of the status line. Static checkers therefore verify that a view returns one of the allowed forms without tying the dictionary to any status representation.

MethodView.__init_subclass__ in src/flask/views.py runs when a subclass is created. If the subclass does not define methods in its own class dictionary, the hook builds a set. It first adds the methods sets from every direct base class that has one, so inherited HTTP methods are kept, then adds the upper-cased name of each method in http_method_funcs that the subclass defines. The result is stored as cls.methods, and this set is what the route registration uses to decide which HTTP verbs the rule accepts. Taking the union avoids dropping inherited handlers when a subclass adds its own. A subclass that sets methods explicitly skips the hook entirely, so the explicit list wins.

UUIDTag in src/flask/json/tag.py exists because JSON has no native UUID type, so a uuid.UUID stored in the session would otherwise be lost or turned into a plain string on the next request. The to_json method returns value.hex, a 32-character hexadecimal string, and to_python returns uuid.UUID(value) built from that string. Because both directions are defined and the tag key marks the value as a UUID, untagging a session reconstructs the original object rather than a string. The hex form is compact, canonical and round-trips exactly, while the tag ensures the restored value keeps its type. This matters for session storage and for any tagged JSON the framework reads back into Python.

AsyncMethodView, which handles async def handlers, inherits from the synchronous MethodView so the two share the same dispatch logic. The base MethodView.dispatch_request looks up the handler for request.method, and the async variant only changes how that handler is called: it wraps the coroutine function so the framework awaits it or runs it through the app's ensure_sync machinery. Reusing the base avoids duplicating method lookup, the methods set built in __init_subclass__, and the decorators handling. Keeping one dispatch path means a bug fix or new behavior appears in both variants at once. The async variant only overrides the parts that differ, which is the usual way Flask adds async support to existing components.

ScriptInfo in src/flask/cli.py accepts two optional arguments, app_import_path and create_app. The import path is used by the command-line tool, which reads FLASK_APP or the --app option as a string such as module:factory. The create_app callable is used when code already has a factory, such as FlaskCliRunner and other embedding code that builds the app in memory. Providing both lets the same ScriptInfo serve the real CLI, where Flask must import the module itself, and tests or tools that already hold a constructed factory, without the caller needing to write the factory to a module. The load_app method checks the callable first and falls back to the import path, so both entry points converge on one loading routine.

The method open_resource in src/flask/sansio/app.py takes a mode argument and raises ValueError unless it is r or rb. The reason is that resources are files shipped with the application package, located under root_path, and the framework treats them as read-only inputs. Allowing write modes would let application code overwrite files inside an installed package, which may be read-only or shared, and would mix configuration assets with mutable data. Restricting the mode keeps the method's contract simple and makes its intent clear: it is a loader for bundled data, not a general file API. Developers who need writable storage are expected to use the instance folder or their own paths instead.

ScriptInfo in src/flask/cli.py stores the result of loading in an attribute such as _loaded_app, and load_app returns the cached object on later calls. Loading is deferred until a command actually needs the app for two reasons. Constructing the ScriptInfo happens while Click parses options, before --help or the group callback has finished, and eager import would run the user's application code and may fail before the user sees a helpful message. Lazy loading also means the FLASK_DEBUG and environment settings read by the group are applied before the app is created. The cache ensures that the factory runs only once in a process, even though many commands and callbacks may ask for the app during one invocation.

The premise is slightly overstated. SecureCookieSession.__getitem__ in src/flask/sessions.py sets self.accessed to True every time a key is read, and this is a plain attribute assignment on each read, not a dictionary mutation. It does not call the on_update callback, so it does not mark the session modified. The performance cost is only a small Python-level attribute write on every read, which is negligible compared with signing and parsing the cookie. The real purpose of the accessed flag is to make the response include a Vary: Cookie header whenever session data was read, so caches know the response depends on the cookie. Signed cookie string conversion happens only on save or load, so frequent reads do not slow that conversion.

The premise is probably mistaken. Calling the blueprint template-filter decorator many times, once per blueprint, adds one entry to the jinja_env.filters dictionary per call and runs its deferred callback once per registration. Each step is a constant-time dictionary insert, so the cost grows linearly with the number of decorator calls and is negligible in practice. Startup work of that size is not a source of slowdown. The blueprint test cases check behavior, namely that the filter is visible to templates rendered from a blueprint and that the record_once mechanism installs it once per app. Their purpose is correctness, not benchmarking, so the repeated calls exist to exercise the logic rather than to stress performance.

The test in tests/test_blueprints.py that checks dotted names builds a Blueprint whose name contains a dot and expects a ValueError. The check lives in the Blueprint constructor in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, which rejects any name containing the character dot. The reason is that the endpoint of a view inside a blueprint is formed as blueprint_name.function_name, and Flask splits endpoints on the dot to find the blueprint. A dot in the blueprint name would make that split ambiguous, so url_for and the blueprint lookup could resolve the wrong endpoint. Rejecting the name at construction gives the developer an immediate error at the point where the name is written, not a confusing routing failure later.

SecureCookieSessionInterface.get_signing_serializer in src/flask/sessions.py builds a new itsdangerous serializer each time it is called, and it is called for every request that loads or saves a session. Building the serializer involves deriving a signing key from the secret key with the chosen key derivation and digest, which runs HMAC operations and so costs CPU on each request. Under high concurrency this derivation repeats for every request even though the secret key does not change, so the same work is done thousands of times per second. The fix is to build the serializer once and reuse it, or to cache the derived key. Because the work is pure CPU and not I/O, it becomes a bottleneck when many threads compete for the interpreter.

TagDict.to_json in src/flask/json/tag.py builds a new dictionary whose keys are copied unchanged and whose values are passed through serializer.tag. JSON object keys must be strings, and the keys of a Python dictionary used in a session are already strings in the normal case, so there is nothing to tag. Tagging the keys would also make the object harder to read and would break the dictionary-based tag format. The class tags values because nested values might be unsupported types such as tuples, UUIDs or bytes that need their own tag. Keys are not tagged, and dictionaries that happen to contain a single key matching a tag name are escaped by TagDict so they are not mistaken for a tag on load.

The test in tests/test_logging.py checks the case where the root logger already has a stream handler. Flask's create_logger, in src/flask/logging.py, adds a default StreamHandler to app.logger only when has_level_handler returns False for the logger. That function walks the logger hierarchy from the app logger upward and checks whether any handler at an effective level exists. If the root logger already has a stream handler, the walk finds it, so no default handler is added. The test therefore asserts that the app logger's handlers list is empty, showing that messages will propagate to the root handler instead of being printed twice. This avoids duplicate log lines when the application configures logging itself.

The transformation happens in the make_config method of src/flask/sansio/app.py, which the App constructor calls to create the config object. If instance_relative_config is set, make_config replaces the root path with self.instance_path, then creates the Config instance with that path and the default values. Config then uses the path to resolve relative file names in from_pyfile and related loaders. So the root path is changed inside make_config before the configuration storage object is created, and the rest of the code sees the instance path only through that config. Without the flag, the root path of the package or module is passed unchanged.

The decision is in FlaskGroup.get_command in src/flask/cli.py. The method first calls the parent Click group to see whether a command is registered directly on the group. Commands loaded from setuptools entry points are added to the group earlier, during initialization through _load_plugin_commands, so they are found by the first step. If the name is not found there, the method asks the application's CLI group, obtained by loading the app through ScriptInfo, and returns the command with that name if the app defines one. The order means built-in and plugin commands take precedence, and application commands are looked up last. The method returns None if none of the three sources has the name.

The tag class for Markup is TagMarkup in src/flask/json/tag.py. Its to_json method calls the __html__ method of the value, which returns the HTML string that markupsafe defines on Markup and other HTML-aware objects, and to_python constructs a Markup object from the stored string. The check method uses callable(getattr(value, '__html__', None)) to detect such values. The lower-level helpers are therefore the __html__ protocol and the markupsafe Markup class, which the tag delegates to rather than implementing HTML escaping itself. The conversion keeps the value's safe-HTML status across a session round trip, so a stored Markup object remains Markup after it is loaded.

TagList in src/flask/json/tag.py implements to_json as a list comprehension that calls self.serializer.tag on each item. The serializer, a TaggedJSONSerializer, owns a dispatcher with an ordered list of tag objects, and its tag method loops over them, calling each tag's check method until one matches. For a nested list, the matching tag is again TagList, so the recursion goes back into to_json for the inner list. Mixed contents such as strings, dictionaries, tuples and bytes are handled because each item is tagged individually by the same dispatcher. If no tag matches, the value is returned unchanged, so plain JSON types pass through without a wrapper. The result is a fully tagged structure that the untagging step reverses on load.

The OPTIONS decision is in add_url_rule in src/flask/sansio/app.py. When provide_automatic_options is not passed, the code reads the attribute of the same name from the view function, which is how View classes set it. If that is still None, the code checks whether OPTIONS is absent from the methods and whether the PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS config value is true; if both hold, it adds OPTIONS to the rule's methods and records the flag on the Rule. At request time, the dispatch code in src/flask/app.py calls make_default_options_response only when a request uses OPTIONS and the rule has the automatic flag set, so a user-defined OPTIONS handler is never replaced. The branch structure therefore combines the per-view flag, the method set and the app config.

The lookup is _find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py. The premise order is slightly wrong. The method first obtains the exception class and any HTTP code through _get_exc_class_and_code. It then loops over codes, trying the specific HTTP code first and then None, which means generic handlers. Inside that loop it loops over the names tuple, which is the active blueprint names followed by None for the app. Only for each of those scopes does it walk exc_class.__mro__ and look up each class in the handler map. So the sequence is HTTP code outermost, then blueprint scopes innermost-first, then the exception MRO innermost. The first match wins.

The test class is in tests/test_helpers.py and is named TestUrlFor. It contains tests that call url_for with an _anchor argument to check the fragment, with _scheme and _external to check the scheme and host in the generated URL, and with methods to check that routing respects the HTTP method. The helpers under test are implemented in src/flask/helpers.py and in the URL building code of src/flask/sansio/app.py. Its location in the helpers test module is consistent with the convention that tests are grouped by the module they exercise. I am not fully certain of the exact class name, so a checker should confirm it against the file.

The encoding flows from the test function in tests/test_helpers.py into Flask.open_resource. The test calls app.open_resource with a resource name, a text mode such as r, and an encoding argument. The method, defined in src/flask/sansio/app.py, validates the mode against the allowed read modes and then joins root_path with the resource name. It opens the joined path with the mode and encoding passed through, so the returned file decodes text as the caller asked. Because the call passes the encoding argument straight into the built-in open function, the test can check that a file with non-ASCII characters is read correctly. I am less certain of the exact parameter forwarding, so this is a best reconstruction.

The base64 decoding for byte tags is TagBytes.to_python in src/flask/json/tag.py. It is invoked during untagging. The loads method of TaggedJSONSerializer calls json.loads with object_hook set to the serializer's untag method. The json module calls that hook for each parsed object from the innermost outward, so every single-key dictionary is passed to untag. untag checks whether the key is one of the registered tag keys, and if so calls the matching tag's to_python method with the value. For the bytes tag, that method runs b64decode and returns bytes. So decoding happens during the object_hook callback, immediately after JSON parsing produces each dictionary.

The inheritance effect is in Config.from_object in src/flask/sansio/config.py. The method iterates over dir(obj), which returns all attributes including those inherited from parent classes, and copies each attribute whose name is all uppercase into the config dictionary. Because dir includes inherited names, a child class sees the parent's configuration keys, and a value that the child redefines overrides the parent's value. If the code used vars or the instance dictionary instead, inherited settings would be missed. Passing a class rather than an instance works because getattr on the class returns its class attributes. The resolution therefore follows normal Python attribute lookup along the method resolution order.

The orchestration is in Flask.wsgi_app and the request context. Flask.wsgi_app creates a RequestContext and calls push, which calls session_interface.open_session to load the session from the request cookie. The session is attached to the context. At the end of the request, the response goes through Flask.process_response, which calls session_interface.save_session with the session object. The session object belongs to exactly one request, so concurrent requests do not share it. Because the session data lives in the signed cookie and not on the server, there is no shared store that the two methods could race on. The only conflict possible is between two responses that set the same cookie, where the browser keeps the last one it receives.

The route handler is in tests/type_check/typing_route.py, and it is a view that returns a list of dictionaries, annotated with a type such as list[dict[str, Any]]. Its route decorator is Flask.route, which is defined in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py and is generic over a TypeVar bounded by Callable returning ResponseReturnValue. The static check is run by mypy with configuration in pyproject.toml, which lists the type-check test directory among the files to analyze. The checker verifies that the decorator preserves the function's signature and that the return annotation is a valid response return type. I am not fully certain of the exact file layout, so this should be confirmed.

The premise is overstated. _find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py walks exc_class.__mro__, which is the class's ancestor list, and for each class it does one dictionary lookup in the handler map. Its cost is therefore proportional to the depth of the exception hierarchy times the number of blueprint scopes and codes checked, and each step is O(1). Typical exception hierarchies are only a few levels deep, so the overhead is small compared with building the response. The method is called only when an error occurs, not on every request. A cache keyed by exception class could reduce repeated lookups, but the linear walk is unlikely to be a measurable bottleneck unless a very deep hierarchy and many blueprints are combined.
